name: Grace Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the dry goods and canned goods buyer at Marlowe Grocers' Supply, a distributor that sells to about 300 small shops and school kitchens across three counties. I'm at my desk by 7:15, ringing suppliers while their warehouses are still quiet. By lunch I've checked what's low, argued about a price per case, and put in orders from my own spreadsheet that I've kept for twenty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the argument, honestly. Getting a tomato canner to drop two cents a case feels like winning something for everybody downstream. What wears me out is the owners. Since the investment firm bought us, every quarter brings a new target and a new dashboard that nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then, because the owners can stop pretending a chatbot will do my job. I'd say it at the break room table and to my sister on the phone. Online I say nothing; I don't trust that crowd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix my real problem. The firm that owns Marlowe has squeezed margins every quarter since it bought us, hype or no hype. I'm 58, I earn less than buyers at the big chains, and there are maybe two other places within an hour's drive that would hire someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep buying for our 300 accounts and keep paying down the mortgage, which still has six years left. I'd also push harder on the union drive among our drivers and buyers, because that's the only protection I really trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's a flat, grey feeling, like standing on a platform where no train comes. I'm not scared of the software. I'm scared of the next owner's spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you earn less than buyers at the big chains. What does that gap mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the car is eleven years old and we don't take holidays. Last winter the boiler packed up and we put 900 on the credit card, and it took until August to clear. That gap is why I'm so loud about the union at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if things got worse here, even though AI hadn't changed much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, no question. They sold our delivery trucks to a contractor and let two buyers go last year. Our owners cut two buyers and called it efficiency. No chatbot did that; people with a spreadsheet and a bonus did.

say: I'd say good: the owners can **stop pretending** a chatbot does my job.
I'd keep pushing the **union drive** among our drivers and buyers.
think: Hype or not, the real threat is **private equity** squeezing margins every quarter.
At 58 on lower pay, with few buyer jobs nearby, I have **nowhere easy** to go.
do: Keep buying for all **300 accounts** and the same spreadsheet.
Put spare money toward the **mortgage**, which still has six years left.
Sign up more buyers and drivers for the **union**.
feel: **Flat and tired**; I fear the next owner's spreadsheet, not the software.
S0.quote: Our owners cut two buyers and called it efficiency. No chatbot did that; people with a spreadsheet and a bonus did.
fieldNote: Blames the owners, not the technology; her anger is about **who holds power**, and it's steady and old.
Thin money and few local buyer jobs keep her worried even when AI changes little.

steps.text: Keep buying canned and dry goods for the 300 small-shop and school accounts
Put every spare 50 a month toward the mortgage
Sign up Marlowe's buyers and drivers for the union drive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work to get the union in now, before the software decides who stays. In my own circle I'd say it's coming for desk jobs first, and we're the desk. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd sign any petition that came my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm one of the first to go. The tool the firm bought already forecasts demand and suggests order quantities, and I ignore it. They'll point to my 20-year spreadsheet one day and ask why a person is still doing this by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my buying exactly as I do and see the targets as they come. I'd ask Sam to take every extra shift as school caretaker. And I'd go to my union meetings, because there's no way I'm learning a chatbot to prove I'm still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cornered. Picture watching a flood come up the road and being told to keep sweeping the porch. I've given my firm twenty years. I'm angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't use the tools. What about the younger buyers on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got Dmitri, 26, and he uses them on the sly. I'd tell him to keep going, because he has time, and I don't. But I'd also tell him the owners will use his work to justify not replacing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours or pay dropped, what gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance gets argued over first, then Noor's help with her nursing loan, which is 150 a month. I'd hate that more than anything. After that it's the heating, and we'd wear coats indoors.

say: I'd tell everyone at work to **join the union** now, before the software decides who stays.
I'd say desk jobs like ours go **first**, and say nothing online.
think: I'm probably one of the **first to go**; the firm's forecasting tool already suggests order quantities.
Owners will use younger buyers' AI work to **justify not replacing** me.
do: Keep buying by hand and go to every **union meeting**.
Ask Sam to take every extra **caretaker shift** at the school.
Refuse to learn the chatbot just to prove I'm useful.
feel: **Cornered and angry**; twenty years given to a firm that sees me as a cost.
S1.quote: Picture watching a flood come up the road and being told to keep sweeping the porch. I've given my firm twenty years.
fieldNote: Stubborn refusal to use AI is a **principled stand** as much as a habit, and it leaves her exposed.
Money worry shows up as specific bills: her daughter's 150 loan help, car insurance, heating.

steps.text: Keep buying by hand from the 20-year spreadsheet
Attend every union meeting and push for a no-layoff clause
Argue down the car insurance and cut the heating to 17 degrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a catastrophe and the government has to step in tonight, with income support and rules on firing. I'd say it loud at the union hall. Two years is nothing. Our local council can't even fix potholes in two years, and I'm 58 with under a month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished, and I'd rather say that to you than to my family. Buying is exactly the thinking work the card describes, and I'm 58 with under a month saved. The robots coming three years later don't help me, because my job goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd call in every favour. I'd ask Marlowe's owners for a severance deal in writing, push the union to bargain for it, and ask the council about retraining even though I'm too old for most of it. I'd move our spending to groceries and the mortgage only, and Sam and I would talk to the bank about holding the payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor has gone. I'd probably lie awake and run numbers on the ceiling. Part of me would be furious and part of me just numb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would two years be enough to do anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to run out of money and not enough to find a new trade at my age. Maybe I'd get 18 months of pay if the union wins a package; without that, six weeks. That's the whole difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Noor and Idris, on the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to panic and not to send money, though I'd be crying inside. I'd say, "Your mother has fought for worse and we will get through this together." Then I'd ring my sister and tell her the truth.

say: I'd call it a **catastrophe** and demand income support and firing rules from government.
I'd say it loud at the **union hall**, not online.
think: Buying is exactly the thinking work AI takes first, so I think I'm **finished**.
Robots three years later don't help me; my job goes on the **stated date**.
do: Ask Marlowe for **severance in writing** and have the union bargain for it.
Cut spending to groceries and the **mortgage** only.
Talk to the bank about **holding** the mortgage payment.
feel: Like the **floor has gone**; furious and numb, awake at night running numbers.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. Our local council can't even fix potholes in two years, and I'm 58 with under a month of savings.
fieldNote: Has **no personal plan**, only collective ones; her whole answer runs through union and government.
Money is the sharp edge: 18 months of severance versus 6 weeks is the gap she keeps returning to.

steps.text: Have the union bargain for 18 months of severance at Marlowe
Cut spending to groceries and mortgage only
Ask the bank to hold the mortgage payment during the gap
Join the union march demanding income support and firing rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us room to win rules, and I'd spend it organising. At work I'd tell people to get their contracts checked and their pensions written down. Online? I might finally post something, but only to share a union petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little less sick than in the two-year one, but only a little. I'd be 63, so I'm hoping the firm keeps me until then. If they cut me at 61, I'd have a pension that's too small and no way to bridge to the state age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at my desk and make myself useful the old way, which is knowing every supplier by name. I'd fight to get the early-retirement terms in the next union contract. I'd save 100 a month by ending the cable and the streaming and wiping out the 900 on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, with a little hope. Dread because I know how these firms behave. Hope because people can organise over five years, and we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew the exact year it would arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count backward from the year it arrives and plan my last day at Marlowe. I'd also work out whether to claim my pension early. I'd also make Sam get his own savings account, because my money is tied up with the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good five years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contract that says buyers can retire at 60 on a fair pension, and that no one gets let go for being 55 or older. That's all I'd ask. And a boiler that doesn't die.

say: I'd say five years gives us room to win **rules**, and I'd spend it organising.
I'd tell colleagues to check their **contracts and pensions** now.
think: I'm hoping the firm **keeps me until 63**; cut at 61, I can't bridge to pension age.
Less sick than the two-year picture, but **only a little**.
do: Fight for **early-retirement terms** in the next union contract.
Save **100 a month** by ending cable and streaming, and clear the card.
Make Sam open his own **savings account**.
feel: **Dread**, with a little hope, because people can organise over five years.
S3.quote: I'd count backward from the year it arrives and plan my last day at Marlowe. I'd also work out whether to claim my pension early.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **countdown plan** aimed at retirement terms, not a new career.
Keeps returning to the contract as her shield; she trusts groups, not tools.

steps.text: Fight for early-retirement terms in the next union contract
Save 100 a month by ending cable and streaming
Plan a last day at Marlowe and price an early pension claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and I'd probably say it doesn't matter to me. I'd be 68, long gone from Marlowe. But I'd say it to the younger buyers and the school kids: demand protection while you still have votes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel safe for myself and sick for Noor and Idris. I'd retire at 65 or so, because the firm will have found a way to trim me before then regardless. The money is the real problem: a thin pension and no cushion, whatever year the AI comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, and I'd put 200 a month into the pension top-up the firm offers, which I've skipped for years. I'd help Dmitri learn what I know about suppliers, because my knowledge walks out the door with me. I'd keep going to union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier than the others. I'd feel steady, with an ache for the next generation. I might even enjoy the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does money still worry you if you have ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years of 200 a month doesn't make a cushion. We'd have maybe a month's rent saved, and my partner's school job could vanish too. Time helps, but it doesn't pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What one piece of advice would you give your young colleague Dmitri?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill that needs hands and trust, like caring work or a trade. I know they may be automated eventually, but that's three years more breathing room than a desk. And join something. Don't face it alone.

say: I'd tell younger buyers to **demand protection** while they still have votes.
For myself I'd say it **hardly matters**, because I'll be long gone.
think: I feel safe for myself, but sick for **Noor and Idris**.
The real problem is a **thin pension** with no cushion, whatever year AI arrives.
do: Put **200 a month** into the firm's pension top-up I've skipped for years.
Teach Dmitri every **supplier relationship** I hold.
feel: **Steadier** than the other pictures, with an ache for the next generation.
S4.quote: My partner's school job could vanish too. Time helps, but it doesn't pay the bills.
fieldNote: Ten years eases her own fear but not her money problem; the **thin cushion** carries the mood.
Wants to pass on her supplier knowledge, which shows pride and a wish for legacy.

steps.text: Put 200 a month into the firm's pension top-up
Teach Dmitri every supplier relationship before retiring
Keep attending union meetings and recruit younger buyers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. Sixty-odd months of mortgage left, under a month's savings, and no time to do anything. What would help is a legal rule that firms must give notice and severance, a pension that bridges to state age, and a union with teeth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stupid for not using the tools. I'm not scared of learning. I'm scared of being told to train my replacement. If someone asked me for my twenty years of supplier knowledge and paid me fairly for it, I'd sit down and teach it tomorrow.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of learning. I'm scared of being told to train my replacement.
portrait: Grace Khan, 58, is the **dry goods buyer** for a distributor serving 300 small shops and school kitchens.
She earns less than buyers at big chains, has **under a month saved**, and sees few similar jobs nearby.
She blames the **private equity owners**, not the technology, and trusts unions over tools; she never uses AI.
Her mood stays worried even when AI changes little, and rises to **panic** in the two-year world.
She'd bargain for **severance**, cut spending and push for early retirement, not retrain.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: no time, under a month saved and a mortgage still running.
whatWouldHelp: A legal rule for **notice and severance**, a pension that bridges to state age, and a union with teeth.
